''S. nigrum'' subsp. ''schultesii''
''S. nigrum'' subsp. ''vulgare'' }} [[File:Morelle noire Vilmorin.jpg|thumb|Illustration "Morelle de l'île de France" in Vilmorin 1925]] [[File: Solanum nigrum berries.jpg|thumb|Ripe berries of ''S. nigrum'']] '''''Solanum nigrum''''', the '''European black nightshade''' or simply '''black nightshade''' or '''blackberry nightshade''',{{Cite book|title=The Weed Forager's Handbook|last1=Grubb|first1=Adam|last2=Raser-Rowland|first2=Annie|publisher=Hyland House Publishing Pty Ltd|year=2012|isbn=978-1-86447-121-2|location=Australia|pages=35}} is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Solanaceae]], native to [[Eurasia]] and introduced in the [[Americas]], [[Australasia]], and [[South Africa]]. Ripe berries and cooked leaves of edible strains are used as food in some locales, and plant parts are used as a traditional [[medicine]]. Some other species may also be referred to as "[[black nightshade]]".{{cite journal|last1=Mohy-ud-dint|first1=A|last2=Khan|first2=Z|last3=Ahmad|first3=M|last4=Kashmiri|first4=MA|title=Chemotaxonomic value of alkaloids in ''Solanum nigrum'' complex|journal=Pakistan Journal of Botany|volume=42|issue=1|pages=653–660|year=2010|url=http://www.pakbs.org/pjbot/PDFs/42(1)/PJB42(1)653.pdf}} ''Solanum nigrum'' has been recorded from deposits of the [[Paleolithic]] and [[Mesolithic]] era of ancient [[Great Britain|Britain]] and it is suggested by the botanist and ecologist [[Edward James Salisbury|Edward Salisbury]] that it was part of the native flora there before [[Neolithic]] [[agriculture]] emerged.{{cite book|last=Salisbury|first=EJ|year=1961|title=Weeds and Aliens|series=New Naturalists Series|publisher=Collins|location=London}} The plant was known and mentioned by ancient [[herbalists]], including [[Dioscorides]].{{cite book|last1=Edmonds|first1=JM|last2=Chewya|first2=JA|title=Black Nightshades, ''Solanum nigrum'' L. and related species|publisher=International Plant Genetic Resources Institute|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nfau8bsLyUUC&q=solanum+nigrum+edmonds&pg=PA93|isbn=978-92-9043-321-7|year=1997}} In 1753, [[Carl Linnaeus]] described six varieties of ''Solanum nigrum'' in ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.{{cite book|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/27049/27049-h/27049-h.htm|last=Linnaeus|first=C|year=1753|title=Species Plantarum IV-V}} ==Description== [[Image:Black Nightshade - Flickr - treegrow (2).jpg|thumb|225px|Black nightshade flowers]] [[Image: Solanum nigrum habit.jpg|thumb|226px|Habit]] Black nightshade is a common herb or short-lived perennial shrub, found in many wooded areas, as well as disturbed habitats. It reaches a height of {{convert|30|to|120|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}}, leaves {{convert|4.0|to|7.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|to|5|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} wide; ovate to heart-shaped, with wavy or large-toothed edges; both surfaces hairy or hairless; [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{convert|1|to|3|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long with a winged upper portion. The flowers have petals greenish to whitish, recurved when aged and surround prominent bright yellow anthers. The berry is mostly {{convert|6|to|8|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, dull black or purple-black.{{cite web|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Solanum~nigrum|title=''Solanum nigrum'' plant profile|work=New South Wales Flora Online}} In India, another strain is found with berries that turn red when ripe.{{cite journal|last1=Venkateswarlu|first1=J|last2=Krishna Rao|first2=M|title=Inheritance of fruit colour in the ''Solanum nigrum'' complex|journal=Proceedings of the Indian Academy of Sciences, Section B|year=1971|volume=74|number=3|pages=137–141|doi=10.1007/BF03050624|s2cid=80921919}} Sometimes ''S. nigrum'' is confused for the more toxic deadly nightshade (''[[Atropa belladonna]]''), which is in a different genus within [[Solanaceae]]. A comparison of the fruit shows that the black nightshade berries grow in bunches, whereas the deadly nightshade berries grow individually. Another distinction is black nightshade flowers have white petals, whereas deadly nightshade flowers have purple petals. ===Growth habit=== The suited soil pH value of black nightshade is between 5.5 and 6.5. Preferring rich organic matter; being well watered and improved verility. However, in the lack of organic matter, poor ventilation (heavy) clay, its roots will be stunted, plant growth is weak and fruiting commodity is therefore poor. It is difficult to grow in high temperatures and high humidity.{{cite journal |last1=Ogg |first1=AG |last2=Rouger |first2=BS |last3=Schiling |first3=EE |title=Characterization of Black Nightshade (''Solanum nigrum'') and Related Species in the United States |journal=Weed Science |date=1981 |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=27–31|doi=10.1017/S0043174500025789 |s2cid=182438916 }} ==Taxonomy== ''Solanum nigrum'' is a highly variable species with many varieties and forms described.[http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/efsa/lucid/Solanaceae/Solanum%20species/key/Australian%20Solanum%20species/Media/Html/Solanum_nigrum.htm ''Solanum nigrum'' Factsheet, South Australian Government] The recognized subspecies are: 1. ''S. nigrum'' L. subsp. ''nigrum'' – glabrous to slightly hairy with appressed non-glandular hairs
2. ''S. nigrum'' L. subsp. ''schultesii'' (Opiz) Wessley – densely hairy with patent, glandular hairs
3. ''S. nigrum'' L. subsp. ''vulgare''{{failed verification|date=September 2024}} – found in cooler regions, has a more spreading habit and its leaves might be more wrinkled compared to the typical subspecies. The '''''Solanum nigrum'' complex''' — also known as '''''Solanum'' L. section ''Solanum''''' – is the group of black nightshade species characterized by their lack of prickles and stellate hairs, their white flowers, and their green or black fruits arranged in an umbelliform fashion. The ''Solanum'' species in this group can be [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomically]] confused, more so by intermediate forms and hybridization between the species. Some of the major species within the ''S. nigrum'' complex are: ''S. nigrum'', ''[[Solanum americanum|S. americanum]]'', ''[[Solanum douglasii|S. douglasii]]'', ''[[Solanum opacum|S. opacum]]'', ''[[Solanum ptychanthum|S. ptychanthum]]'', ''[[Solanum retroflexum|S. retroflexum]]'', ''[[Solanum sarrachoides|S. sarrachoides]]'', ''[[Solanum scabrum|S. scabrum]]'', and ''[[Solanum villosum|S. villosum]]''. ==Toxicity== [[File:Solanum_nigrum_leafs_flowers_fruits.jpg|thumb|left|Leaves, flowers and fruit of ''S. nigrum'']] [[Solanine]] levels in ''S. nigrum'' have been tested, and the plant is rarely fatal.{{cite book|last=North|first=P|year=1977|title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi in Colour|publisher=Blandford Press|pages=140–141}} Solanine poisoning symptoms may occur when immature green fruit or mature leaves are ingested raw. There is typically a delay of 6 to 12 hours after ingestion for symptoms to occur.{{cite journal |last1=Schep|first1=LJ|last2=Slaughter|first2=RJ|last3=Temple|first3=WA |title=Contaminant berries in frozen vegetables |journal=The New Zealand Medical Journal |volume=122 |issue=1292 |pages=95–6 |date=April 3, 2009|pmid=19448780 |url=http://natlib.govt.nz/records/20744815?search%5Bi%5D%5Bcategory%5D=Journals&search%5Bi%5D%5Bsubject%5D=Solanum+nigrum&search%5Bpath%5D=items |access-date=2 May 2017}} Initial symptoms of toxicity include [[fever]], sweating, [[vomiting]], abdominal pain, diarrhea, confusion, and [[drowsiness]].{{cite web|url=http://www.inchem.org/documents/pims/plant/solanum.htm|title=''Solanum nigrum'' profile|work=IPCS|publisher=INCHEM}} Death from ingesting large amounts of the plant results from [[cardiac arrhythmia]]s and [[respiratory failure]]. Livestock have also been poisoned from nitrate toxicity by grazing the mature leaves and green berries of ''S. nigrum''. In central Spain, the [[great bustard]] (''[[Otis tarda]]'') may act as a seed disperser of European black nightshade (''Solanum nigrum'').{{cite journal |last1=Bravo |first1=C. |last2=Velilla |first2=S. |last3=Bautista |first3=L.M. |last4=Peco |first4=B. |year=2014 |title=Effects of great bustard (''Otis tarda'') gut passage on black nightshade (''Solanum nigrum'') seed germination |journal=Seed Science Research |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=265-271 |url=https://digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/97149/7/97149_posprint_LuisMBautista.pdf |hdl=10261/97149 |hdl-access=free |s2cid=32739044 |doi=10.1017/S0960258514000178}} Black nightshade is highly variable, and some advice says to avoid eating the berries unless they are a known edible strain.{{cite book|last1=Turner|first1=NJ|last2=von Aderka|first2=P|title=The North American guide to common poisonous plants and mushrooms|publisher=Timber Press|pages=181–182|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bmGY5APFfFQC&q=Nancy+J.+Turner+solanum+nigrum&pg=PA182|isbn=978-0-88192-929-4|year=2009}} The toxin levels may also be affected by the plant's growing conditions. The [[toxin]]s in ''S. nigrum'' are most concentrated in the unripe green berries, and immature fruit should be treated as toxic.{{cite book|last=Tull|first=D|title=Edible and Useful Plants of Texas and the Southwest— A Practical Guide|publisher=University of Texas Press|year=1999|isbn=978-0-292-78164-1}} Most cases of suspected poisoning are due to consumption of leaves or unripe fruit. There are [[ethnobotanical]] accounts of ''S. nigrum'' young leaves and shoots being boiled as a vegetable with the cooking water being discarded and replaced several times to remove toxins. Solanine is practically insoluble in water and can be destroyed by boiling but not by baking. ''S. nigrum's'' leaves may be different from this perspective. Young cooked leaves of Solanum complex sp. are a source of many useful nutrients similar to levels found in spinach.{{cite web | url=https://pfaf.org/user/plant.aspx?LatinName=Solanum+nigrum | title=Solanum nigrum Black Nightshade, Common Nightshade, Poisonberry, Black Nightshade PFAF Plant Database }} Solanum complex berries have been consumed since ancient times. ==Uses== [[File:Makoi or Solanum nigrum berries.jpg|thumb|225px|Ripe berries of the "Red Makoy", which is an edible variety of ''S. nigrum'']] Some of the uses ascribed to ''S. nigrum'' in literature may actually apply to other black nightshade species within the same species complex, and proper species identification is essential for food and medicinal uses (see ''Taxonomy'' section). ===Culinary use=== ''S. nigrum'' has been widely used as a food since early times, and the fruit was recorded as a [[famine food]] in 15th-century China.{{cite book|last=Read|first=BE|year=1977|title=Famine Foods of the Chiu-Huang Pen-ts'ao|publisher=Southern Materials Centre|location=Taipei}} Despite toxicity issues with some forms, the ripe berries and boiled leaves of edible strains are eaten. The thoroughly boiled leaves – although strong and slightly bitter flavours – are used like spinach as [[horta (food)|horta]] and in [[fataya]] pies and [[quiche]]s. The ripe black berries are described as sweet and salty, with hints of [[liquorice]] and [[melon]].{{cite book|last=Irving|first=M|title=The Forager Handbook — A Guide to the Edible plants of Britain|publisher=[[Ebury Press]]|year= 2009|isbn=978-0-09191-363-2}} In [[Kenya]], among the [[Kisii people|Abagusii]], ''S. nigrum'' ({{lang|guz|rinagu}} – singular; {{lang|guz|amanagu}} – plural) is a vegetable delicacy which when blanched and sauteed or boiled to soften and then salted or sauteed and eaten with [[Ugali]] (a corn meal dish). In the rest of Kenya, ''S. nigrum'' (managu) is eaten in a similar way. In [[Tanzania]], ''S. nigrum'' ({{lang|sw|mnafu}} or {{lang|sw|mnamvu}} in [[Swahili language|Kiswahili]]) is a popular green vegetable. Sautéed with chicken or pork, eaten with [[Ugali]], it is an expensive meal in most restaurants in urban areas. Traditionally, the [[Iraqw people]] in northern Tanzania have used ''S. nigrum'' ({{lang|irk|manakw}}) as vegetable for generations, eaten with special 'ugali' ({{lang|irk|xwante}}), stiff porridge made with [[Maize|corn]], [[millet]] or [[sorghum]] flour. An [[ethnobotanical]] survey conducted in the mid 1990s on the islands of [[Zanzibar]] and [[Pemba Island|Pemba]] indicated that ''S. nigrum'' was referred to as {{lang|sw|vwevwe}} in [[Swahili language|Kiswahili]].{{cite book |last1=Heine |first1=Bernd |last2=Legère |first2=Karsten |title=Swahili Plants: An Ethnobotanical Survey |date=1995 |publisher=Rüdiger Köppe Verlag and Köln |location=Cologne |isbn=3-927620-89-0 |page=305}} In [[India]], the berries are casually grown and eaten, but not cultivated for commercial use. In South India, the leaves and berries are routinely consumed as food after cooking with [[tamarind]], onion, and [[cumin]] seeds.{{Cite journal|title = Ethnobotanical investigations among tribes in Madurai District of Tamil Nadu (India)|date = 2006-05-11|url= |journal = [[Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine]]|volume = 2|page = 25|last = Ignacimuthu|first = S|others = M Ayyanar, Sankara Sivaraman K|doi = 10.1186/1746-4269-2-25|pmid = 16689985|pmc = 1475842 | doi-access=free }} The berries are referred to as "fragrant tomato". Although not very popular across much of its growing region, the fruit and dish are common in Tamil Nadu ([[:ta:மணத்தக்காளி|மணத்தக்காளி]] in [[Tamil language|Tamil]]), Kerala, southern Andhra Pradesh, and southern Karnataka. They are used not only fresh but also dried. In [[Ethiopia]], the ripe berries are picked and eaten by children. During famines, all affected people would eat berries. In addition, the leaves are collected by women and children, who cook the leaves in salty water and consume them like any other vegetable. Farmers in the [[Konso Special Woreda]] report that because ''S. nigrum'' matures before the maize is ready for harvesting, it is used as a food source until their crops are ready.{{cite web|url=http://www.africa.upenn.edu/faminefood/category2/cat2_Solanium_nigrum.htm|title="Wild Food" Plans with "Famine Foods" Components: ''Solanum nigrum''|work=Famine Food Guide}} The [[Welayta people]] in the nearby [[Wolayita Zone]] do not weed out ''S. nigrum'' that appears in their gardens since they likewise cook and eat the leaves.{{cite conference|last=Zemede|first=Asfaw|url=http://www.bioversityinternational.org/publications/Web_version/500/ch08.htm|title=Conservation and use of traditional vegetables in Ethiopia|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120707210646/http://www.bioversityinternational.org/publications/Web_version/500/ch08.htm |archive-date=2012-07-07|conference=Proceedings of the [[IPGRI]] International Workshop on Genetic Resources of Traditional Vegetables in Africa|location=Nairobi|date=29–31 August 1995}} In [[Ghana]], they are called ''kwaansusuaa'', and are used in preparing various soups and stews, including the popular [[palm nut soup]] commonly eaten with ''[[Banku (dish)|banku]]'' or ''[[fufu]]''.{{cite journal|last1=Asibey-Berko|first1=E|last2=Tayie|first2=FAK|title=Proximate analysis of some under-utilized Ghanaian vegetables|journal=Ghana Journal of Science|volume=39|pages=91–96|url=http://www.ajol.info/index.php/gjs/article/viewFile/15862/16335}} [[File:Solanum Nigrum Berries.jpg|thumb|left|Ripe and unripe ''S. nigrum'' berries of the (red-berried) variety that grows in India]] In [[South Africa]], the very ripe and hand-selected fruit (''{{lang|af|nastergal}}'' in [[Afrikaans]] and ''{{lang|zu|umsobo}}'' in [[Zulu language|Zulu]]) is cooked into a runny purple jam.{{cite journal|last=Jansen van Rensburg|first=WS|display-authors=etal|url=http://ajol.info/index.php/wsa/article/view/49110/0|title=African leafy vegetables in South Africa|journal=[[Water SA]]|volume=33|issue=3|pages=317–326|year=2007|doi=10.4314/wsa.v33i3.180589|doi-access=free|hdl=2263/4875|hdl-access=free}} However, the fruit used in South Africa is more likely to be [[Solanum retroflexum]].{{cite web | url =https://dsae.co.za/entry/umsobosobo/e07492 | title = umsobosobo, noun | last = | first = | date = | website =Dictionary of South African English | publisher = | access-date =9 April 2021 | quote = }} In Greece and Turkey, the leaves are called ''{{lang|el-Latn|istifno}}'', and in [[Crete]] known as ''stifno''. They are one of the ingredients included in the salad of [[boiled greens]] known as [[Horta (food)|''horta'']].{{cite web|website=Organically Cooked|title=Amaranth – vlita – and black nightshade – stifno (Βλήτα και στίφνος)|year=2008|url=http://www.organicallycooked.com/2008/06/amaranth-vlita-and-black-nightshade.html|access-date=2012-08-09|archive-date=2023-01-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230123111237/http://www.organicallycooked.com/2008/06/amaranth-vlita-and-black-nightshade.html}} In [[Indonesia]], the young fruits and leaves of cultivated forms are used and are known as ''{{lang|jv|ranti}}'' ([[Javanese language|Javanese]]) or ''{{lang|su|leunca}}'' ([[Sundanese language|Sundanese]]). The fruit and leaves are eaten raw as part of a traditional salad [[lalab|''lalapan'']], or the fruit is cooked (fried) with ''[[oncom]]''.{{cite web|url=http://sehat-gayaku.blogspot.com.au/2010/07/leuncaranti.html|website=Sehat itu anugerah|title=Leunca/ranti|year=2010}} It was imported into Australia in the 1850s as a vegetable during the [[Australian gold rushes#Notable gold finds which started rushes|gold rush]], but ''S. nigrum'' is now prohibited for trade as a food by the [[Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code]].{{cite web|work=Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code|title=Standard 1.4.4 – Prohibited and Restricted Plants and Fungi|date=7 December 2015 |publisher=Australian Government|url=http://www.comlaw.gov.au/Details/F2008B00621}} During ancient times in [[Hawaiian Islands|Hawaii]] young shoots, leaves, small white flowers, and small black berries were eaten.{{Cite web | url=http://wehewehe.org/gsdl2.85/cgi-bin/hdict?a=q&r=1&hs=1&m=-1&o=-1&e=q-11000-00---off-0hdict--00-1----0-10-0---0---0direct-10-ED--4-------0-1lpm--11-haw-Zz-1---Zz-1-home-papolo--00-3-1-00-0--4----0-0-11-00-0utfZz-8-00&q=popolo&j=pm&af=1&fqf=ED |title = Nā Puke Wehewehe ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi |website=wehewehe.org}} The leaves, among other greens, were cooked by rolling hot stones among them in a covered gourd.Thrum, Manoa Valley, Hawaiian Annual 1892 ===Medicinal usage=== The plant has a long history of medicinal usage, dating back to medieval Greece, "... In the fourteenth century, we hear of the plant under the name of Petty Morel being used for canker and with Horehound and wine taken for [[dropsy]]."{{cite book|last=Grieve|first=M|title=A Modern Herbal|publisher=Penguin|year=1984|pages=582–583}} It was a traditional European medicine used as a strong [[sudorific]], [[analgesic]] and [[sedative]] with powerful [[narcotic]] properties, but was considered a "somewhat dangerous remedy".{{cite book|last1=Schauenberg|first1=P|last2=Paris|first2=F|title=Guide to Medicinal Plants|publisher=Keats Publishing Inc|year=1977|page=53}} Internal use has fallen out of favor in [[Western world|Western]] [[herbalism]] due to its variable [[chemistry]] and toxicity, but it is used topically as a treatment for [[herpes zoster]].{{cite journal|last1=Nohara|first1=T|last2=Ikeda|first2=T|last3=Fujiwara|first3=Y|last4=Matsushita|first4=S|last5=Noguchi|first5=E|last6=Yoshimitsu|first6=H|last7=Ono|first7=M|display-authors=4|title=Physiological functions of solanaceous and tomato steroidal glycosides|journal=Journal of Natural Medicines|volume=61|number=1|pages=1–13|doi=10.1007/s11418-006-0021-y|year=2006|s2cid=36689200}}{{cite journal|last1=Ikeda|first1=T|last2=Ando|first2=J|last3=Miyazono|first3=A|last4=Zhu|first4=XH|last5=Tsumagari|first5=H|last6=Nohara|first6=T|last7=Yokomizo|first7=K|last8=Uyeda|first8=M|display-authors=4|title=Anti-herpes virus activity of Solanum steroidal glycosides|journal=Biological & Pharmaceutical Bulletin|date=March 2000|volume=23|issue=3|pages=363–4|doi=10.1248/bpb.23.363|pmid=10726897|doi-access=free}}{{cite journal|last1=Nohara|first1=T|last2=Yahara|first2=S.|last3=Kinjo|first3=J|title=Bioactive Glycosides from Solanaceous and Leguminous Plants|journal=Natural Product Sciences|year=1998|volume=4|issue=4|pages=203–214}}{{cite book|editor-last=Schmelzer|editor-first=GH|title=PROTA: Medicinal Plants 1|year=2008}} There is much disagreement as to whether the leaves and fruit of ''S. nigrum'' are poisonous, but there are countries that grow this plant as a food crop. The toxicity of ''S. nigrum'' may vary by region and species.{{cite journal |last1=Jimoh |first1=FO |last2=Adedapo |first2=AA |last3=Afolayan |first3=AJ |title=Comparison of the Nutritional Value and Biological Activities of the Acetone, Methanol and Water Extracts of the Leaves of ''Solanum nigrum'' and ''Leonotis leonorus'' |journal=Food and Chemical Toxicology |date=2010 |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=964–971 |doi=10.1016/j.fct.2010.01.007 |pmid=20079394 }} [[Native Hawaiians]] use the berries' juice as a laxative, they also boil young leaves to relieve sore throats and coughs.{{cite magazine|title=Healing Plants: Pōpolo – Foundation of the Hawaiian Pharmacy|first=Barbara|last=Fahs|issue=May–June 2014|magazine=Ke Ola|url=https://keolamagazine.com/plants/popolo/|access-date=28 October 2022|date=May 2014}} ''S. nigrum'' is an important ingredient in traditional Indian medicines. Infusions are used for [[dysentery]], [[stomach]] complaints, and [[fever]].{{cite book|last=Jain|first=SK|year=1968|title=Medicinal Plants|publisher=Thomson Press (India) Ltd|pages=133–134}} The juice of the plant is used on [[ulcer]]s and other skin diseases. The fruits are used as a [[Herbal tonic|tonic]], [[laxative]], [[appetite]] stimulant, and for treating [[asthma]] and "excessive thirst". Traditionally the plant was used to treat [[tuberculosis]].{{cn|date=March 2023}} This plant's leaves are used to treat mouth ulcers that are common during winter in [[Tamil Nadu]], India. In North India, the extracts of boiled leaves and berries are also used to alleviate liver-related ailments, including jaundice. The juice from its roots is used against asthma and whooping cough.{{cite journal|journal=Studies on Ethno-Medicine|volume=2|issue=1|pages=39–45|year=2008|title=Traditional Phytotherapy among the Nath People of Assam|first1=M|last1=Sikdar|first2=U|last2=Dutta|url=http://www.krepublishers.com/02-Journals/S-EM/EM-02-0-000-08-Web/EM-02-1-000-08-Abst-PDF/EM-02-1-039-08-030-Sikdar-M/EM-02-1-039-08-030-Sikdar-M-Tt.pdf|doi=10.1080/09735070.2008.11886313|s2cid=54662164}} ''S. nigrum'' is also widely used in oriental medicine where it is considered to be antitumorigenic, [[antioxidant]], anti-inflammatory, [[hepatoprotective]], [[diuretic]], and [[antipyretic]].{{cite journal|last1=Jain|first1=R|last2=Sharma|first2=A|last3=Gupta|first3=S|last4=Sarethy|first4=IP|last5=Gabrani|first5=R|title=''Solanum nigrum'': current perspectives on therapeutic properties|journal=Altern Med Rev|date=Mar 2011|volume=16|issue=1|pages=78–85|url=http://www.altmedrev.com/publications/16/1/78.pdf|pmid=21438649|access-date=2011-05-06|archive-date=2016-07-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160705043006/http://www.altmedrev.com/publications/16/1/78.pdf}}{{cite journal |last1=Gubarev |first1=M. A |title=Plant-derived glycoalkaloids protect mice against lethal infection with Salmonella typhimurium|journal=Phytotherapy Research|date=1998 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=79–88|doi=10.1002/(SICI)1099-1573(199803)12:2<79::AID-PTR192>3.0.CO;2-N |s2cid=83679181 }} Some experiments indicate that the plant can inhibit growth of [[cervical carcinoma]] in mice.{{cite journal|last1=Jian|first1=L|last2=Qingwang|first2=L|last3=Tao|first3=F|last4=Kun|first4=L|year=2008|title=Aqueous extract of ''Solanum nigrum'' inhibit growth of cervical carcinoma (U14) via modulating immune response of tumor bearing mice and inducing apoptosis of tumor cells|journal=Fitoterapia|volume=79|issue=7–8|pages=548–556|doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2008.06.010|pmid=18687388}} The alkaloid [[solanine]], seems to inhibit the proliferation of different cancer cells in vitro, such as breast and pancreatic cancer. Experiments on several different cell lines resulted in "a viable approach to inhibit inflammation and carcinogenesis and to prevent cancer."{{cite journal | title = Anti-inflammatory potential of native Australian herbs polyphenols | author = Yu Guo | author2 = Karunrat Sakulnarmrat | author3 = Izabela Konczaka | journal = Toxicology Reports| year = 2014 | volume = 1 | pages = 385–390 | doi = 10.1016/j.toxrep.2014.06.011 | pmid = 28962255 | pmc = 5598408}} Uttroside B, a saponin, was identified as a bioactive chemotherapeutic agent, against hepatocellular carcinoma, obtained from the methanolic extract of ''S. nigrum''.{{cite journal | doi=10.1038/srep36318 | doi-access=free| title=Evaluation of uttroside B, a saponin from Solanum nigrum Linn, as a promising chemotherapeutic agent against hepatocellular carcinoma | year=2016 | last1=Nath | first1=Lekshmi R. | last2=Gorantla | first2=Jaggaiah N. | last3=Thulasidasan | first3=Arun Kumar T. | last4=Vijayakurup | first4=Vinod | last5=Shah | first5=Shabna | last6=Anwer | first6=Shabna | last7=Joseph | first7=Sophia M. | last8=Antony | first8=Jayesh | last9=Veena | first9=Kollery Suresh | last10=Sundaram | first10=Sankar | last11=Marelli | first11=Udaya K. | last12=Lankalapalli | first12=Ravi S. | last13=Anto | first13=Ruby John | journal=Scientific Reports | volume=6 | article-number=36318 | pmid=27808117 | pmc=5093766 | bibcode=2016NatSR...636318N | s2cid=4966820 }} Lankalapalli et al. isolated uttroside B and provided its structure elucidation by derivatization, which afforded an enol ether, and characterized by detailed 2D NMR analysis in this publication. Uttroside B and uttroside A can be differentiated by the group present in C-22 with hydroxyl and methoxy groups, respectively. The structural resemblance of uttroside B and uttroside A poses a challenge in differentiation of these two molecules by NMR or other techniques. Recently, this group provided a correction of a NMR figure with respect to the structure of uttroside B, which enable differentiation of uttroside B from uttroside A with characteristic chemical shift difference in 13C NMR of hemiketal carbon C-22 at 110.5 and 112.5 ppm, respectively.{{cite journal | doi=10.1038/s41598-020-77440-0 | doi-access=free| title=Author Correction: Evaluation of uttroside B, a saponin from Solanum nigrum Linn, as a promising chemotherapeutic agent against hepatocellular carcinoma | year=2020 | last1=Nath | first1=Lekshmi R. | last2=Gorantla | first2=Jaggaiah N. | last3=Thulasidasan | first3=Arun Kumar T. | last4=Vijayakurup | first4=Vinod | last5=Shah | first5=Shabna | last6=Anwer | first6=Shabna | last7=Joseph | first7=Sophia M. | last8=Antony | first8=Jayesh | last9=Veena | first9=Kollery Suresh | last10=Sundaram | first10=Sankar | last11=Marelli | first11=Udaya K. | last12=Lankalapalli | first12=Ravi S. | last13=Anto | first13=Ruby John | journal=Scientific Reports | volume=10 | issue=1 | page=20431 | pmid=33208836 | pmc=7676244 | s2cid=227065139 }} US-FDA granted an orphan drug designation for uttroside B against hepatocellular carcinoma. ==Cultivation== Black nightshade is cultivated as a food crop on several continents, including Africa and North America. The leaves of cultivated strains are eaten after cooking. A garden form with fruit about {{convert|1.27|cm|in|abbr=on}} diam. is occasionally cultivated.{{cite web|title=Wonderberry|publisher=Center for New Crops & Plant Products, Purdue University|url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/Crops/Wonderberry.html}} ==Weed== Black nightshade can be a serious agricultural [[weed]] when it competes with [[crops]].{{cite thesis|last=Taab|first=A|year=2009|url=http://pub.epsilon.slu.se/2064|title=Seed dormancy and germination in ''Solanum nigrum'' and ''S. physalifolium'' as influenced by temperature conditions|institution=Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences}}{{cite journal|last1=Keeley|first1=PE|last2=Thullen|first2=RJ|year=1991|title=Biology and Control of Black Nightshade ''(Solanum nigrum)'' in Cotton ''(Gossypium hirsutum)''|journal=Weed Technology|volume=5|pages=713–722|number=4|jstor=3986881|doi=10.1017/S0890037X00033741|s2cid=89885270 }} It has been reported as a weed in 61 countries and 37 crops.
